title: A curve-sample figure asks what shapes a rate coefficient can take while staying inside its stated uncertainty
summary: A rate coefficient is a line on an Arrhenius plot. Its uncertainty is a band around that line. Three Arrhenius parameters can vary, so the samples inside the band can be parallel shifts, tilts about a pivot, or curved arches. The figures show which of these a sampling rule produces and whether samples respect the limits.

media.alt: Lines on axes of 1 over T from 0.0004 to 0.0012 against a value near 26 to 27. A solid black nominal line and two dashed black limit lines rise to the right. A straight green line sits parallel to the nominal, a red line with markers forms an arch touching the upper limit and ending on the lower limit, and a dashed blue curve runs from the lower limit at the left to the upper limit at the right.

source.caption: Chapter 4. Class-A, class-B and class-C Arrhenius curves between the uncertainty limits, reaction 2HO2 = H2O2 + O2
source.note: Six Chapter 4 figures about how a single reaction's rate coefficient can vary inside its uncertainty. The representative figure overlays one example curve of each of three sampling classes, A, B and C, between uncertainty limits for the reaction 2HO2 = H2O2 + O2. Figures 20, 21 and 22 show many samples of one class each for another reaction (R9a). Figure 15 shows the effect of perturbing only the pre-exponential factor versus all three Arrhenius parameters, and figure 17 overlays the limits on experimental rate data for reaction R1 from a database.

read_the_figure.question: What family of rate-coefficient curves does each sampling rule produce, and do they all stay inside the uncertainty limits?
read_the_figure.axes: x: inverse temperature (1/T in the class figures, 1000/T in figure 15 and 17). y: the logarithm of the rate coefficient (the label says rate constant, but the values are of the size expected for ln k). Black solid or blue solid: nominal. Dashed or dotted black: uncertainty limits. Coloured lines: samples.
look_at: Class A samples are straight lines parallel to the nominal line: only the vertical offset changes. They fill the band uniformly in height.

Class B in the representative figure is an arch: the curve touches an upper limit in the middle of the range and the lower limit at both ends. Its shape is not a straight line, so curvature in 1/T has been introduced.

Class C samples are tilted lines that cross the nominal line at different pivot points, with different slopes. Figure 22 shows the fan: lines rotate about the middle of the range and spread at the ends.
The limits. In figures 20 and 21 every sample stays inside; in figure 22 a few lines leave the band at the cold end. That is the single most important thing to check.

Figure 15 compares perturbing only the pre-exponential factor (a blue parallel shift) with perturbing all parameters (a red line that crosses the nominal at a pivot near 0.8 in 1000/T). Figure 17 puts the nominal and limits over the scatter of experimental rate data for reaction R1: the data follow the nominal closely at both ends and scatter widely in between, with a number of points above the upper limit.
read_the_figure.proves: That the family of curves implied by the sampling rule is physically sensible (smooth, within limits) and that the limit lines are a real constraint on all of them. It does not prove the limits themselves are right.
if_wrong: Samples outside the limits: the sampling domain is bigger than the ellipsoid that defines the limits.
All samples clustered at the limits or at the centre: the sampling rule over- or under-weights the boundary.
Class A only: samples cannot change slope, so any temperature-dependent effect on the rate is lost.
Curves with kinks: the temperature grid used for plotting is too coarse.
must_check: The y axis states whether the quantity is k or ln k.
The x axis is stated (1/T versus 1000/T) and the same in the figures compared.
The limit lines are drawn on every figure and the legend says how they are computed.
The number of samples drawn is stated.
The class definitions are given where the classes are used.

terms.meaning: The three numbers of the modified Arrhenius form: pre-exponential factor, temperature exponent and activation energy.
The natural logarithm of the rate coefficient, linear in 1/T when n is zero.
The rate coefficient with parameters at their recommended values.
The upper and lower curves bounding the allowed variation of the rate coefficient with temperature.
A matrix L with Sigma = L L^T that turns standard random numbers zeta into correlated parameter deviations.
The temperature at which a perturbed curve crosses the nominal curve, so that the deviation changes sign.
One rule for choosing the random vector zeta. The figures show the curves each rule produces.

remember: Three parameters make three degrees of freedom of curve shape.
A pure A perturbation is a parallel shift on a log plot.
A change of activation energy tilts the line about a pivot.
A sample's curve at temperature T depends on only a projection of the parameter vector.
The limit curves are an envelope, not a sample.

steps.title: The modified Arrhenius form in the log
steps.note: The log of the rate coefficient is linear in the three parameters (ln A, n, E_a/R). That linearity is what makes the covariance picture simple.

steps.title: Write it as a dot product
steps.tex: \kappa(T)=\boldsymbol\theta(T)^{\top}\mathbf p,\quad \boldsymbol\theta=\bigl(1,\ \ln T,\ -1/T\bigr)^{\top},\quad \mathbf p=\bigl(\ln A,\ n,\ E_a/R\bigr)^{\top}
steps.note: Each temperature picks a direction theta(T) in parameter space. A perturbation of the parameters changes the curve at T by theta dotted with the perturbation.

steps.title: A perturbation of the curve
steps.note: With a covariance matrix Sigma = L L^T the deviation of the parameters is L zeta, where zeta holds independent standard random numbers. This is the form printed in the legend of the representative figure.

steps.title: Why the limits are an envelope
steps.note: By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, any zeta inside a ball of radius zeta_max keeps the curve within a band of half-width zeta_max times the norm of L^T theta at every temperature. This is consistent with the dashed limit curves, and it explains why samples with larger zeta leave the band.

steps.title: A parallel shift versus a tilt
steps.note: Perturbing only A gives a constant delta, a parallel shift (class A and the blue curve in figure 15). Perturbing E_a adds a term linear in 1/T, which tilts the line. A change of n adds curvature.

steps.title: The pivot of a tilted line
steps.note: A perturbed straight line crosses the nominal at x*, where the deviation changes sign. In figure 15 this is where the red and black curves cross.

steps.title: Sampling inside the ball
steps.note: Any sampling rule is a rule for the direction u and radius rho. A rule that fills the interior gives many curves near the nominal, one that concentrates near the boundary gives curves near the limits.

worked.title: Pivot of a tilted perturbation
worked.problem: A perturbation of ln k on the 1000/T axis is delta = 0.6 - 0.75 x, with x = 1000/T in inverse kelvin times 1000. Where is the pivot, and on which side of it is the perturbed curve above the nominal?

solution.text: Check the sign on each side.

worked.answer: The pivot is at x = 0.8 (T = 1250 K). The perturbed curve is above the nominal at higher temperatures (smaller x) and below it at lower temperatures. The numbers were chosen to match the crossing seen in figure 15. They are not read from a fit.

analyze.q: Class A samples are all parallel to the nominal line. Which Arrhenius parameter can they not be varying, and what does that imply for how the sampled rate behaves at different temperatures?
analyze.hint: Which term of delta kappa is constant?

analyze.q: In figure 22 some class-C curves leave the band at the cold end. Give two explanations and one check.
analyze.hint: zeta larger than zeta_max; sampling in parameter space instead of curve space.

analyze.q: Figure 17 shows experimental points scattered outside the limits in the middle of the range. What does it say about the prior uncertainty, and what would a tuning that uses this reaction do?

evaluate.q: Which sampling class would you use if you wanted every sample to be physically plausible at all temperatures, and why?
evaluate.hint: Samples inside the limits at every T.

evaluate.q: A sampler that gives only parallel shifts is cheap and simple. What systematic error does it introduce into an uncertainty propagation that depends on temperature?

create: Redraw the three classes as small multiples on shared axes with the same number of samples each, the limits shaded, and the nominal in bold. Colour any curve that leaves the band red.
Design a test that counts, for each class, the fraction of samples that stay inside the limits at all temperatures.

checks.q: Why is a change of only the pre-exponential factor a parallel shift on the plot?
checks.answer: Because ln k contains ln A as a constant term. Changing A adds the same amount to ln k at every temperature, so the line moves vertically without changing slope.

checks.q: A perturbed line has delta ln k = 0.4 - 0.5 x on the 1000/T axis. Where does it cross the nominal?
Why do class-C curves in figure 22 spread more at the ends than in the middle?
checks.answer: Tilted lines rotate about a pivot near the middle, so their deviation from the nominal grows linearly with distance from the pivot and is largest at the ends.

checks.q: A sample exits the limits. Is the sampler wrong?
checks.answer: Not necessarily: the limit is a bound on a ball of zeta values. If the sampler draws outside that ball, exits are expected. Whether that is desirable depends on whether the limits are meant as hard bounds.

checks.q: How would you draw samples that are uniform in the area between the limits at one fixed temperature?
checks.hint: Sample the curve value, not the parameters.
checks.answer: Draw the value of ln k at that temperature uniformly between the limits, then choose any parameter vector that produces it. The resulting curves are not uniform at other temperatures, which is the trade-off.
